payload.rationale: Resolution requires the GISS unsmoothed LOTI for 2026 to exceed both the 2025 value and 1.28°C (the 2024 record). Observed background: 2024 set the GISS record at ~1.28°C; 2025 came in slightly below (roughly 1.24–1.27°C) despite no El Niño, showing a very elevated baseline. Transfer assumptions: late 2025/early 2026 featured weak La Niña/neutral conditions, which typically hold early-2026 months somewhat below 2024's pace; seasonal outlooks during 2026 pointed toward a developing El Niño in the second half of the year. El Niño usually boosts global temperature most in the year after onset (as in 2023→2024), so 2026 would more likely land near or just under the record, with 2027 the stronger record candidate. Pre-year forecasts (e.g., Met Office, Berkeley Earth) placed 2026's central estimate near 2024/2025 levels with record odds roughly 15–35%. The threshold is tight (needs ≥1.29°C), so the outcome hinges on how quickly and strongly El Niño warmth emerges in Sep–Dec 2026 and whether early-2026 months ran warmer than expected. Too high: if the first half of 2026 ran near 2025 levels (~1.2°C) and El Niño onset was slow, reaching an annual 1.29°C is difficult even with a warm Q4. Too low: the underlying warming trend (~0.2–0.25°C/decade, possibly accelerated by aerosol reductions) plus a rapidly strengthening El Niño could push late-2026 monthly anomalies to 1.4–1.5°C, easily lifting the annual mean past 1.28°C; several scientists (e.g., Hansen's group) argued 2026 could set a record. I have no observed 2026 monthly data through the September cutoff, so I settle near 0.3.
limitations: No supplied evidence; no access to GISS monthly anomalies for 2026 through the cutoff date.
Exact 2025 GISS value and ENSO evolution in 2026 are recalled approximately, not observed.
Outcome is sensitive to a small margin (~0.01–0.05°C) and to late-year El Niño timing.
